topic: Earth in the Solar System & Its Motions

items.question: Explain how the rotation and revolution of the Earth, together with the inclination of its axis, give rise to day and night and to the sequence of seasons.
items.modelAnswer:
The Earth's climatic rhythms flow from two simultaneous motions combined with a fixed axial tilt. **Rotation** — the daily west-to-east spin about an axis inclined **66½° to the orbital plane (23½° from the vertical)** — completes in about **24 hours** and produces **day and night**, the lit and dark halves being separated by the **circle of illumination**, which never coincides with the axis because of the tilt. Rotation also generates the **Coriolis effect**, deflecting winds and currents.

**Revolution** — the Earth's year-long journey around the Sun in an **elliptical orbit of 365¼ days** — would by itself change nothing seasonal; it is the **constant 23½° tilt** that matters. As the Earth revolves, different latitudes receive the Sun's vertical rays: on the **summer solstice (21 June)** the Sun is overhead at the **Tropic of Cancer**, giving the Northern Hemisphere its longest day and 24-hour daylight at the Arctic Circle; on the **winter solstice (22 December)** it is overhead at the **Tropic of Capricorn**. At the **equinoxes (21 March, 23 September)** the Sun is over the **equator**, giving equal day and night worldwide. Because the tilt keeps the same hemisphere leaning sunward for part of the orbit, the hemispheres experience **opposite seasons**, and the poles undergo roughly six months of day followed by six months of night.

For a tropical state like **Andhra Pradesh** (~12.5°–19.9°N, just south of the Tropic of Cancer), the high angle of the noon sun year-round explains its warm climate and modest seasonal temperature range, while the revolution-driven shift of the overhead sun underlies the onset and retreat of its monsoon. Thus rotation gives the day, revolution gives the year, and the axial tilt converts that year into a march of seasons.
keyPoints: Rotation (~24 h, west→east) causes day and night; circle of illumination offset from the axis due to tilt.
Axis inclined 66½° to orbital plane = 23½° from vertical — the tilt, not the ellipse, drives seasons.
Revolution: elliptical orbit of 365¼ days (leap year every 4 years).
Solstices: 21 Jun (Sun over Tropic of Cancer) and 22 Dec (over Tropic of Capricorn); equinoxes 21 Mar & 23 Sep (over equator).
Hemispheres get opposite seasons; poles get ~6 months day then ~6 months night.
AP angle: tropical location → warm year-round, revolution-linked monsoon onset/retreat.

items.question: Bring out the significance of latitudes and longitudes in locating places, classifying climates and reckoning time, with reference to India.
items.modelAnswer:
**Latitudes** and **longitudes** form the coordinate grid by which any point on Earth is precisely located — their intersection fixes a place. **Latitudes** are parallels running 0°–90° north and south of the **equator (0°)**, each degree spanning about **111 km**; the key parallels — **Tropic of Cancer (23½°N)**, **Tropic of Capricorn (23½°S)**, **Arctic and Antarctic Circles (66½°)** — delimit the **heat zones**: the **Torrid** zone between the tropics (overhead sun, hottest), the **Temperate** zones up to the polar circles, and the **Frigid** zones beyond. Latitude thus underpins the classification of temperature and, broadly, climate.

**Longitudes** are meridians running 0°–180° east and west of the **Prime Meridian at Greenwich**, converging at the poles. Their prime role is **time-reckoning**: since the Earth turns **360° in 24 hours**, it covers **15° per hour** and **1° in four minutes**, so places east of Greenwich are ahead and those to the west behind. The **International Date Line** near 180° marks the change of calendar day.

For **India**, the grid is decisive. The country stretches from about **8°N to 37°N**, so the **Tropic of Cancer bisects it**, giving a largely tropical-to-subtropical climate. Its longitudinal spread from ~68°E to ~97°E creates nearly a **two-hour local-time gap** between the western and eastern extremities; to avoid confusion India adopts a single **Indian Standard Time based on 82½°E**, making **IST = GMT + 5:30**. Andhra Pradesh, lying near this standard meridian, keeps clock time close to its true solar time. Latitude and longitude therefore serve at once as tools of **location, climatic classification and standardised timekeeping**.
keyPoints: Intersection of a latitude and a longitude uniquely locates a place.
Latitudes (0°–90° N/S, 1°≈111 km) define heat zones: Torrid, Temperate, Frigid.
Longitudes (0°–180° E/W of Greenwich) reckon time: 15°/hour, 1° = 4 minutes; IDL ≈ 180°.
India ~8°N–37°N: Tropic of Cancer bisects it → tropical/subtropical climate.
~68°E–97°E gives a ~2-hour east–west local-time gap; single IST fixed at 82½°E (GMT+5:30).
AP lies near 82½°E, so its clock time is close to local solar time.
